planting.note: Set out transplants in spring after soil has warmed, or direct sow in fall into prepared beds; this coastal-prairie native tolerates seasonally wet clay and needs no coddling once established.

directions: Plant in full sun in beds with average to seasonally moist soil, spacing plants about a foot apart so the slender branching stems can fill in as a airy clump. Once roots are established this Texas and Louisiana coastal-prairie native shrugs off summer heat, humidity, and short dry spells with little care. Each stem carries small drooping yellow rays around a dark cone from summer into fall, drawing bees, skipper butterflies, and other pollinators. Its narrow habit and long bloom window make it a good filler among grasses in a Gulf Coast wildflower meadow or rain garden edge.

planting.note: Transplant divisions or nursery starts into consistently moist to wet soil after the last frost; this brackish-marsh native spreads by rhizome and needs damp ground to establish.

directions: Set plants in full sun along the margins of ponds, ditches, or rain gardens where soil stays consistently moist to occasionally brackish, giving the twining stems something low to scramble over. Native to Gulf Coast marshes and estuary edges from Texas to Florida, it produces arrowhead-shaped leaves and funnel-form pink-lavender flowers through the warm months that attract bees and sphinx moths. It is an excellent choice for stabilizing damp, low-lying ground where few other flowering vines will thrive. Once rooted it tolerates both standing water after storms and short dry spells between rains.

common_name: Brenthurst Tropical Sage (Pink Bicolor Salvia coccinea)

planting.note: Transplant after all danger of frost once soil has warmed; this reseeding tropical sage selection thrives in the long hot summers of the Gulf Coast.

directions: Transplant into well-drained beds in full sun to light shade, spacing plants a foot or so apart to let the branching stems fill out over the season. This soft-pink-and-white bicolor selection of the Gulf Coast native tropical sage blooms nonstop from late spring until frost and is a magnet for hummingbirds and long-tongued bees. It tolerates heat, humidity, and brief drought far better than most bedding salvias, and readily self-sows to return the following year. Use it in cottage borders or pollinator plantings where its pastel spikes contrast nicely with the more common red-flowered forms.

common_name: Snow Nymph Tropical Sage (White Salvia coccinea)

planting.note: Transplant after the last frost into warm soil; this pure-white tropical sage selection performs best through the long humid Gulf Coast growing season.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in average, well-drained garden soil, giving each plant about a foot of room to branch into a loose mound. This all-white selection of the Gulf Coast native tropical sage lights up evening gardens and pairs well with red or purple companions, while still drawing hummingbirds, bees, and butterflies all summer long. It handles heat and humidity with ease, needs little supplemental water once rooted, and will often reseed itself in beds along the coast. Deadheading spent spikes encourages continuous rebloom from late spring through the first fall frost.

common_name: Pam Puryear Turk's Cap (Pink-Flowered Native Turk's Cap)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plants in spring once frost danger has passed; this soft-pink heirloom Turk's cap selection roots easily and establishes quickly in Gulf Coast heat.

directions: Plant in a bed with morning sun and afternoon shade, or in dappled light beneath trees, and water regularly the first season until the woody base is established. Discovered and popularized by Texas plantswoman Pam Puryear, this selection of the native Turk's cap bears the same twisted pink-red hibiscus-like blooms as the species but in a softer pink shade, opening continuously from late spring through fall. Hummingbirds visit the flowers constantly and songbirds eat the small apple-flavored fruits that follow, making it a dependable wildlife shrub for shady Gulf Coast gardens. It dies back in hard winters but resprouts reliably from the roots each spring.

common_name: Augusta Duelberg Mealy Blue Sage (White Native Salvia farinacea)

planting.note: Transplant in spring into well-drained soil; this vigorous white companion selection to Henry Duelberg sage tolerates Gulf Coast heat, humidity, and clay far better than typical bedding salvias.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained beds, spacing plants roughly two feet apart to allow the upright flower spikes room to develop into a substantial clump. Selected as a white-flowered companion to the popular Henry Duelberg sage, this native Texas mealy blue sage cultivar sends up tall wands of pure white blooms from late spring through fall that are constantly worked by bumblebees and other pollinators. It is markedly more heat-, humidity-, and drought-tolerant than common bedding salvias, making it a long-lived perennial anchor for Gulf Coast borders. Cutting plants back hard in late winter keeps the clump full and floriferous the following season.

subcategory: Gulf Coast native woodland pollinator perennial

planting.note: Set divisions or transplants into humus-rich, partly shaded soil in spring; this woodland native spreads gently by rhizome once established under Gulf Coast tree canopy.

directions: Plant in a woodland-edge or partly shaded bed with rich, moisture-retentive soil, spacing plants a foot or so apart so the clumps can knit together as a groundcover. Native to bottomland woods and shaded ravines across the Gulf South, this smooth-leaved wild petunia bears pale lavender trumpet flowers from late spring through fall that attract bees and serve as a larval host for buckeye and other butterflies. It spreads gradually by rhizome to form an attractive, low-maintenance patch under high shade where turf struggles. Established plantings tolerate both the wet spells and brief dry stretches typical of Gulf Coast summers.

planting.note: Transplant in spring near a trellis or fence in full sun; like the species, this white-flowered form spreads by root suckers and tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity with ease.

directions: Plant along a fence, arbor, or trellis in full sun to light shade in ordinary garden soil, giving the vigorous vine plenty of vertical room to climb by tendril. This pure-white-flowered selection of the native maypop produces the same intricate, fringed blossoms as the wild form but without the usual purple banding, and still serves as the essential host plant for gulf fritillary and zebra longwing caterpillars. Bees and other pollinators visit the large flowers freely, and edible yellow-green fruit follows in late summer. Once established it spreads by root suckers and tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought better than almost any other flowering vine on the Gulf Coast.
